h1: Beer with Nepali and Tibetan food from thukpa to sel roti
title: Beer with Nepali and Tibetan Food | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair beer with Nepali and Tibetan dishes, from thukpa and momos to sukuti and sel roti, with simple style suggestions that work in India.
teaser: Thukpa is a warm broth and sel roti is a sweet ring of fried rice dough. Beer can sit beside both.
standfirst: Himalayan food is easy to find in Indian cities and surprisingly good with beer. Here is how to pick a style for noodle soup, momos, dried meat and a festive sweet.
sections:
Nepali and Tibetan cooking share a mountain kitchen. Both use noodles, dumplings, potatoes, rice and lentils, with butter and mild spice rather than heavy chilli. Indian cities from Delhi to Bengaluru have many places serving the dishes.

  • Thukpa is a noodle soup, usually with vegetables or meat in a clear, gingery broth.
  • Momos are steamed or fried dumplings, usually served with a tomato and chilli dipping sauce called achar.
  • Dal bhat is lentils with rice and vegetables, the daily meal in Nepal.
  • Sukuti is dried, spiced meat, often fried and eaten as a bar snack.
  • Sel roti is a ring-shaped bread made from rice flour batter, fried in oil or ghee and eaten at festivals such as Tihar.

Much of this food is vegetarian or easily made so, which suits many Indian readers. Dal bhat in particular is gentle and balanced, so a light lager or wheat beer is enough beside it.

A bowl of thukpa is warm, savoury and gentle, with a little ginger and garlic. That is a different challenge from heavy curry. A bold beer would flatten it.

A clean, light lager or a pilsner suits the clear broth. A wheat beer is another good partner because its soft body and light citrus lift the ginger. Keep the beer cool but not icy, since very cold beer tastes thin beside a hot soup. Pause between sips of broth and sips of beer so each can be tasted.

Momos vary a lot. A steamed chicken or vegetable momo is mild and juicy. A fried momo is richer. The achar adds sharp tomato, chilli and sometimes sesame or timur, a Himalayan pepper with a tingling citrus note.

  • Steamed momos: a pilsner or a pale lager. The carbonation cleans the palate between bites.
  • Fried momos: an amber lager or a pale ale with moderate bitterness. The malt meets the fried edge.
  • Spicy achar: a wheat beer or a lightly hopped pale ale. Avoid very bitter IPAs, which sharpen the chilli.

Our guide to Indian food and beer pairing and the one on pairing basics explain the principles used here.

Dried spiced meat is salty, chewy and savoury. It asks for a beer that can cleanse the palate. A malty amber lager works well. So does a brown ale or a dark lager with gentle roast. The malt sweetness balances the salt and the carbonation clears the fat.

Fried potatoes in spice and roasted peanuts behave similarly. They are comfortable matches for lager or wheat beer. They make good starters for a group tasting.

Sel roti is lightly sweet, crisp outside and soft within, with a hint of ghee and sometimes cardamom or banana in the batter. It is eaten for breakfast or as a festival snack, not usually as a dessert after a meal.

A malt-forward beer is the natural partner: an amber ale, a brown ale or a dunkel. The toasty, biscuity flavours echo the fried dough. Sweetness in the food makes beer taste drier and more bitter, so avoid hoppy styles here. Keep pours small.
Regional notes and a home tasting

A good rule of thumb is to match the beer to the strength of the dish. Light dishes get light beers. Rich, fried or spiced dishes get a little more malt or carbonation. Himalayan food is rarely very hot, so you have room to try more styles than you would with a fiery curry.

For a home tasting, order a few dishes and pick three beers: a pilsner, a wheat beer and an amber lager. Pour small measures, taste each dish with each beer and write short notes. Our guide to beer with South Indian food follows the same method for another cuisine.

Offer water, have alcohol-free options on the table and never drive afterwards. A long meal with small pours is the best way to taste.
Pairing is only a guess until you can name what you taste. Being able to say "this beer has biscuit sweetness and little bitterness, so it will sit well with fried dough" turns pairing into a skill.
faqs: A pilsner or pale lager for steamed momos, an amber lager or moderately bitter pale ale for fried ones. Choose a wheat beer when the achar is spicy.
Can I drink beer with thukpa?
Yes. A clean lager or wheat beer suits the light broth. Keep the beer cool rather than icy.
A ring-shaped bread of rice flour batter, fried in oil or ghee. It is a festival food in Nepal and parts of the Himalayan region.
Timur is a Himalayan pepper used in Nepali cooking. It has a citrusy, slightly numbing quality.
